sectionTitle: Use of amount of substance in relation to volumes of gases (chemistry only) (HT only)

specStatements.text: Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
The volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20o C and 1 atmosphere pressure) is 24 dm³ .
The volumes of gaseous reactants and products can be calculated from the balanced equation for the reaction.
calculate the volume of a gas at room temperature and pressure from its mass and relative formula mass
calculate volumes of gaseous reactants and products from a balanced equation and a given volume of a gaseous reactant or product
change the subject of a mathematical equation.

scopeNotes.statement: under the same conditions of temperature and pressure
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every comparison of gas volumes in this content is made between gases held at the same temperature and the same pressure, and each stem says so explicitly. No item asks what happens to a gas volume when the temperature or the pressure is changed, and no item uses the ideal gas equation, a pressure-volume relationship or the Avogadro constant, none of which appear in this section of the specification.

scopeNotes.statement: The volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20o C and 1 atmosphere pressure) is 24 dm³ .
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only molar gas volume used anywhere in this content is 24 dm³ per mole at room temperature and pressure, the value the specification supplies. It is treated as a value to be recalled, never derived. No molar volume for other conditions is taught; 22.4 dm³ appears only as a distractor, and its rationale names it as belonging to conditions this specification does not use.

scopeNotes.statement: The volumes of gaseous reactants and products can be calculated from the balanced equation for the reaction.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Volume ratios are taken only from the balancing numbers of species shown as gases. Where an equation contains a solid or a liquid, state symbols are printed in the stem so the student can tell from the given equation alone which species contribute a gas volume; no knowledge of boiling points is needed. Every equation used is balanced, and every equation needed is supplied rather than being asked for.

concepts.term: equal amounts in moles occupy equal volumes
concepts.definition: Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure. What fixes the volume of a gas is the number of moles of particles present, not the mass of the sample and not the size of the individual molecules.
The stated conditions of 20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure, at which the molar gas volume of 24 dm³ applies. Gas volumes may only be converted using 24 dm³ per mole when the gas is at these conditions.
The volume occupied by one mole of any gas. At room temperature and pressure this is 24 dm³ per mole, so volume in dm³ = amount in mol × 24.
The amount of a substance in moles is found from amount (mol) = mass (g) ÷ relative formula mass. This is the first step in turning a mass of gas into a volume at room temperature and pressure.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms shown in the formula of a substance. For a gas made of molecules such as O2 the whole molecule counts, so Mr(O2) = 32, not 16.

concepts.term: mole ratio from a balanced equation
concepts.definition: The balancing numbers in a balanced symbol equation give the ratio of the amounts in moles of the substances that react and that are formed.

Because equal amounts in moles of gases occupy equal volumes under the same conditions, the balancing numbers of the gaseous species also give the ratio of their volumes directly. Volumes of gases may therefore be scaled without converting to moles first, provided every gas involved is at the same temperature and pressure.

concepts.term: changing the subject of an equation
concepts.definition: Rearranging a relationship so that the required quantity stands alone on one side. A quantity that multiplies on one side becomes a division when it is moved to the other side, and a quantity that divides becomes a multiplication.

misconceptions.question: Two flasks of different gases at the same temperature and pressure hold the same volume. What must be equal about the two samples?
misconceptions.correct: The amounts in moles are equal.
misconceptions.misconception: Equal masses of two gases occupy equal volumes, so matching the masses matches the volumes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass is the quantity students can see on a balance, and in earlier work 'how much' almost always meant mass, so mass is carried over as the quantity that must be matched.
misconceptions.correction: Volume is fixed by the amount in moles. 2 g of hydrogen and 2 g of oxygen are very different amounts in moles, so they occupy very different volumes.

misconceptions.question: One mole of sulfur dioxide and one mole of nitrogen are at the same temperature and pressure. Which occupies the larger volume?
misconceptions.correct: Neither; the two volumes are the same.
misconceptions.misconception: A gas with heavier or larger molecules takes up more room per mole than a gas with small, light molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Particle diagrams of solids and liquids show particles touching, so students picture gas molecules as packed together and conclude that bigger molecules need a bigger box.
misconceptions.correction: In a gas the molecules are far apart, and the space between them rather than their own size sets the volume, so one mole of any gas occupies the same volume under the same conditions.

misconceptions.question: What volume does one mole of any gas occupy at room temperature and pressure?
misconceptions.misconception: The molar gas volume is 22.4 dm³ per mole.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 22.4 dm³ is the molar volume at 0 °C and 1 atmosphere and appears in many textbooks and online sources, so it is recalled in place of the value this specification gives for room temperature and pressure.
misconceptions.correction: This specification uses room temperature and pressure, 20 °C and 1 atmosphere, at which the volume of one mole of any gas is 24 dm³.

misconceptions.question: In what unit is the molar gas volume at room temperature and pressure given?
misconceptions.misconception: The size of the molar gas volume is remembered wrongly: the value 24 is given the wrong unit (24 cm3) or the wrong place value (e.g. 2.4 dm3), rather than 24 dm3 per mole.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gas volumes in practical work are read off gas syringes in cm³, so cm³ becomes the automatic unit and the unit given in the specification is overwritten.
misconceptions.correction: The molar gas volume at room temperature and pressure is 24 dm³ per mole, which is 24 000 cm³ per mole. A gas syringe reading of 24 cm³ is only 0.001 mol.

misconceptions.question: How is the volume of a gas at room temperature and pressure found from the amount in moles?
misconceptions.correct: Multiply the amount in moles by 24.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide the amount in moles by 24, or quote 24 dm³ whatever the amount of gas present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most mole calculations students have met involve dividing (mass ÷ Mr, moles ÷ volume for concentration), so dividing becomes the default move whenever 24 appears.
misconceptions.correction: One mole occupies 24 dm³, so more moles means more volume: volume (dm³) = amount (mol) × 24. Dividing would make a larger amount of gas give a smaller volume.

misconceptions.question: A sample of carbon dioxide has a mass of 8.8 g (Mr = 44). What is the first step in finding its volume at room temperature and pressure?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the mass by the relative formula mass to get the amount in moles.
misconceptions.misconception: A gas's mass in grams is read straight off as its amount in moles (grams treated as the number of moles), so the relative formula mass is never used to convert mass to moles; the raw gram figure is then fed into the calculation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'volume = amount × 24' is remembered as 'volume = number × 24', and the only number in the question is the mass, so the mass is used in place of the amount.
misconceptions.correction: Only an amount in moles may be multiplied by 24. Convert first: 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.2 mol, then 0.2 × 24 = 4.8 dm³.

misconceptions.question: What relative formula mass should be used for oxygen gas in a mole calculation?
misconceptions.misconception: Oxygen gas has a mass of 16, the value read straight from the periodic table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The periodic table gives the relative atomic mass of the atom, and students take that number without checking the formula of the substance, which for oxygen gas is O2.
misconceptions.correction: Use the formula of the substance as it appears in the equation. Oxygen gas is O2, so Mr = 2 × 16 = 32.

misconceptions.question: In CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g), which species contribute to the volume of gas produced?
misconceptions.correct: Only the carbon dioxide, because it is the only gas.
misconceptions.misconception: Every substance in the equation occupies 24 dm³ per mole, so solids and liquids count towards the gas volume too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'one mole occupies 24 dm³' is remembered without the word 'gas', so it is applied to any substance in the equation whatever its state symbol.
misconceptions.correction: The molar volume of 24 dm³ applies to gases only. Read the state symbols and include only species labelled (g).

misconceptions.question: N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). 30 cm³ of nitrogen reacts fully. What volume of ammonia forms?
misconceptions.misconception: Gas volumes are conserved one for one, so 30 cm³ of a reactant gives 30 cm³ of a product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is a strong prior rule and gets transferred to volume, and the balancing numbers are read as decoration rather than as a ratio.
misconceptions.correction: Mass is conserved but the number of gas molecules is not. The balancing numbers give the volume ratio: 1 volume of N2 gives 2 volumes of NH3, so 30 cm³ gives 60 cm³.

misconceptions.question: 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g). What volume of oxygen reacts with 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide?
misconceptions.misconception: The ratio is applied the wrong way round, or the balancing number of a third species is used, so the volume is scaled up instead of down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The student picks up whichever balancing number is nearest, or scales in the direction that makes the number bigger, without tracking which species the number belongs to.
misconceptions.correction: Write the ratio with the species named: CO : O2 is 2 : 1, so the oxygen volume is half the carbon monoxide volume, 50 cm³.

misconceptions.question: volume (dm³) = amount (mol) × 24. How is this rearranged to make the amount the subject?
misconceptions.misconception: To get the amount in moles from a gas volume, the relationship volume = amount x 24 is rearranged wrongly: the 24 is subtracted (amount = volume - 24), the expression is flipped (amount = 24 / volume), or the volume is multiplied by 24 instead of divided (amount = volume x 24).
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging is remembered as 'move it across and change the sign', a rule learned for equations built by addition, and it is then applied to an equation built by multiplication.
misconceptions.correction: A quantity that multiplies on one side divides on the other. Since volume = amount × 24, dividing both sides by 24 gives amount = volume ÷ 24.

misconceptions.question: Two gases in a balanced equation are at the same temperature and pressure. Must their volumes be converted to moles before the ratio is used?
misconceptions.correct: No; the volumes are in the same ratio as the balancing numbers.
misconceptions.misconception: Every gas volume must be divided by 24 before the equation can be used, even when only volumes are given and asked for.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The molar volume is the most memorable item in the topic, so 24 is inserted into every gas calculation whether or not a mass or an amount in moles is involved.
misconceptions.correction: Equal amounts in moles occupy equal volumes, so for gases at the same conditions the balancing numbers scale the volumes directly. The 24 is needed only when a mass or an amount in moles is involved.

misconceptions.question: volume = (mass ÷ Mr) × 24. How is this rearranged to make mass the subject?
misconceptions.misconception: The mole calculation is set up upside down: the amount is found by dividing the relative formula mass by the mass (Mr / mass) instead of mass / Mr, or the whole mass-volume conversion is inverted (e.g. mass = volume / (Mr x 24)) - multiplication and division are swapped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two steps are undone in one move rather than one at a time, so a quantity that was dividing is left dividing instead of being brought up to multiply.
misconceptions.correction: Undo one step at a time. Multiply both sides by Mr, then divide by 24: mass = volume × Mr ÷ 24.

mcqs.stem: A sealed flask contains 4.0 g of helium gas, He (Ar = 4). Which sample of methane gas, CH4 (Mr = 16), occupies the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: 4.0 g of helium is 1 mol and 16 g of CH4 is 1 mol. Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
Chosen by students who think the larger methane molecules take up more room each, so a smaller mass would fill the same volume; 4.0 has been divided by 16.
Chosen by students who match the masses, treating mass rather than amount in moles as the quantity that fixes the volume of a gas.
Comes from multiplying the helium mass by the relative formula mass of methane, 4.0 × 16, instead of matching the amounts in moles.

mcqs.stem: Two gas syringes are held at the same temperature and pressure. One contains 0.50 mol of nitrogen, N2 (Mr = 28), and the other contains 0.50 mol of sulfur dioxide, SO2 (Mr = 64). Which statement about the two gas volumes is correct?

options.text: The sulfur dioxide has the larger volume, as its molecules are heavier.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who picture gas molecules as touching, so that heavier, larger molecules must each need more space.

options.text: The two volumes are the same, because the amounts in moles are equal.
options.rationale: Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, whatever the gas.

options.text: The nitrogen has the smaller volume, as it is the lighter gas here.
options.rationale: Applying m02 (heavier molecules take up more room per mole), the lighter nitrogen is judged to occupy LESS space, so its volume is thought smaller - missing that equal amounts in moles of any gas occupy equal volumes at the same temperature and pressure.

options.text: The volumes cannot be compared, as the two masses are different.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe mass is the quantity that fixes gas volume, so unequal masses must make the comparison impossible.

mcqs.stem: What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure)?

options.rationale: 22.4 dm³ is the molar volume at 0 °C, not at the room temperature and pressure this specification uses.
The right number in the wrong unit; gas syringes read in cm³, but the molar gas volume is 24 dm³, which is 24 000 cm³.
The specification states that the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure) is 24 dm³.
A misremembered figure, produced by shifting the decimal point in the recalled value.

mcqs.stem: A balloon holds 3.0 mol of argon gas at room temperature and pressure. What is the volume of the gas in the balloon?

options.rationale: The molar gas volume itself, quoted without scaling it up to the 3.0 mol actually present.
3.0 × 22.4, using the molar volume at 0 °C instead of the 24 dm³ that applies at room temperature and pressure.
24 has been divided by 3.0, turning the relationship upside down; that would make a larger amount of gas occupy a smaller volume.
One mole occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure, so volume = 3.0 × 24 = 72 dm³.

mcqs.stem: A sample of carbon dioxide gas, CO2 (Mr = 44), has a mass of 8.8 g. What is the volume of this sample at room temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: 8.8 × 24, using the mass in grams in place of the amount in moles; only an amount in moles may be multiplied by 24.
Amount = 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.2 mol, and volume = 0.2 × 24 = 4.8 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.
8.8 ÷ 24, dividing by the molar gas volume instead of multiplying, and skipping the conversion to moles altogether.
44 ÷ 8.8 = 5 mol, then 5 × 24; the mass and the relative formula mass have been divided the wrong way round.

mcqs.stem: What is the volume of 4.0 g of oxygen gas, O2, at room temperature and pressure? (Ar of O = 16)

options.rationale: Uses 16 rather than 32, taking the relative atomic mass of the oxygen atom instead of the relative formula mass of the O2 molecule.
4.0 × 24, treating the mass in grams as though it were already the amount in moles.
4.0 ÷ 24, dividing the mass by the molar gas volume instead of converting to moles and then multiplying.
Mr(O2) = 32, so amount = 4.0 ÷ 32 = 0.125 mol and volume = 0.125 × 24 = 3.0 dm³.

mcqs.stem: At room temperature and pressure, volume (dm³) = amount of substance (mol) × 24. A student has measured the volume of a gas in dm³ and wants the amount in moles. Which step gives the amount in moles?

options.text: Subtract 24 from the volume in dm³.
options.rationale: 'Move it across and change the sign' has been applied to a quantity that multiplies, so subtraction has replaced division.

options.text: Multiply the volume in dm³ by 24.
options.rationale: This repeats the operation in the original equation instead of undoing it, so the amount is never made the subject.

options.text: Divide the volume in dm³ by 24.
options.rationale: The 24 multiplies the amount, so dividing both sides by 24 makes the amount the subject: amount = volume ÷ 24.
The division has been written upside down, so a larger measured volume would wrongly give a smaller amount of gas.

mcqs.stem: For a gas at room temperature and pressure, volume (dm³) = (mass (g) ÷ Mr) × 24. A student knows the volume and the Mr of the gas and wants its mass. Which pair of steps gives the mass?

options.text: Multiply the volume by the Mr, and then divide by 24.
options.rationale: Undoing one step at a time gives mass = volume × Mr ÷ 24: the Mr was dividing so it now multiplies, and the 24 was multiplying so it now divides.

options.text: Multiply the volume by 24, then divide by the Mr.
options.rationale: Mr and 24 have swapped roles; the 24 was multiplying so it must divide, and the Mr was dividing so it must multiply.

options.text: Divide the volume by the Mr, then divide by 24.
options.rationale: Both operations have been inverted together, leaving the Mr dividing when it should have been brought up to multiply.

options.text: Divide the volume by 24 and then by the Mr.
options.rationale: Every operation has simply been turned into a division, a sign that the rearrangement was guessed rather than worked through.

mcqs.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). A student wants to use this equation to work out gas volumes at room temperature and pressure. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only the carbon dioxide has a gas volume here.
options.rationale: The molar gas volume of 24 dm³ applies to gases only, and the state symbols show that carbon dioxide is the one gas in this equation.

options.text: Every substance shown occupies 24 dm³ per mole.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who apply the molar gas volume to every species in the equation, ignoring the state symbols.

options.text: The calcium oxide also occupies 24 dm³ per mole.
options.rationale: Calcium oxide is labelled (s), so it is a solid and the molar gas volume does not apply to it.

options.text: The calcium carbonate also occupies 24 dm³ per mole.
options.rationale: Applying m08 (every substance in the equation occupies the molar gas volume, so solids count too), the student assigns 24 dm3 per mole to the solid calcium carbonate as well, instead of recognising that only the carbon dioxide gas has a molar gas volume.

mcqs.stem: Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). 30 cm³ of nitrogen reacts completely with excess hydrogen. What volume of ammonia is formed, measured at the same temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: 30 cm³ has been divided by 24, as though the molar gas volume were needed; it is not, because both quantities here are gas volumes at the same conditions, so the balancing numbers scale them directly.
The gases are at the same conditions, so the balancing numbers give the volume ratio directly: N2 : NH3 is 1 : 2, so 30 × 2 = 60 cm³.
Assumes gas volume is conserved one for one, treating the balancing numbers as decoration rather than as a ratio.
The balancing number 3 belongs to hydrogen, not to ammonia, so 30 × 3 scales by the wrong species.

mcqs.stem: Carbon monoxide burns in oxygen: 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g). What volume of oxygen reacts completely with 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide, both gases measured at the same temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: The ratio has been used the wrong way round; the 2 belongs to carbon monoxide, so the oxygen volume is the smaller one.
100 cm³ has been divided by 24, converting a volume to an amount that is not needed; the molar gas volume plays no part when both quantities are gas volumes at the same conditions.
At the same temperature and pressure the balancing numbers give the volume ratio: CO : O2 is 2 : 1, so 100 ÷ 2 = 50 cm³.
Assumes the volumes must match one for one, ignoring the 2 : 1 ratio given by the balanced equation.

mcqs.stem: Ethene burns completely: C2H4(g) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(l). 20 cm³ of ethene burns in excess oxygen. What volume of carbon dioxide is produced, measured at room temperature and pressure?

options.rationale: Counts the water as a gas as well, adding 2 volumes of H2O to the 2 volumes of CO2; the state symbol (l) shows the water is liquid.
Assumes gas volume is conserved one for one, so the product volume is taken to equal the reactant volume.
Scales by the 3 in front of the oxygen, which is the wrong species; the ratio needed is ethene to carbon dioxide.
C2H4 : CO2 is 1 : 2 among the gases, so 20 × 2 = 40 cm³ of carbon dioxide.
